notes:
I've written notes on all 22 verses. A few limits first:

- **Tradition labels.** The only page that tagged a commentator with a tradition was StudyLight, which calls John Gill "Baptist · Calvinism." Otherwise I've named the commentator without assigning a denomination.
- **Disagreements.** The clearest disagreements I found don't split along denominational lines. They're between individual commentators, mainly over whether the people's request was hypocritical (vv. 2–3, 20) and why Jeremiah waited ten days (v. 7).
- **Not found.** I didn't find a Haydock or other Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter, any Bible Odyssey or NET Bible notes, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace treatment. I couldn't open Precept Austin, and I found nothing from Wesley's own notes.

---

**Chapter overview**
- Guzik summarises the chapter as a polite request covering a decision already made: the people had settled on Egypt and wanted God to approve it. He shows us how their polite request masks a predetermined decision — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- Keil and Delitzsch see two parts to God's answer: a promise to build them up and protect them if they stay (vv. 9–12), and a threat that they will die by sword, famine and plague if they go to Egypt (vv. 13–18). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm

**v. 1**
- After the massacre at Mizpah (ch. 41), the anxious survivors and their leaders asked Jeremiah for a word from the Lord. Guzik quotes Cundall: this had never happened in the forty years before Jerusalem fell. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- Guzik also quotes Feinberg: this Hoshaiah may be the one named in the Lachish Letters. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- **Jezaniah or Azariah (a text question).** The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint, LXX) reads "Azariah" here, the name the Hebrew gives in 43:2.
  - Ellicott thinks Azariah may be Jezaniah's brother, though LXX's reading is possibly the true one.
  - Barnes thinks LXX is probably right and that a scribe changed the name to match the list in ch. 40.
  - Keil and Delitzsch think the opposite: the error is more likely in 43:2.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-1.htm
- Calvin says the two leaders are named to honour them as the chief men. On "from the least to the greatest," he says it was not a plot of a few: everyone had already resolved on Egypt yet came to the prophet as if honestly. — https://studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/42-1.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-42.html
- Calvin adds that coming to the prophet made them more guilty than going straight to Egypt would have. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-42.html
- Bible.org (Utley) calls "small and great" an exaggerated, all-inclusive idiom that doesn't mean literally every person. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-42

**v. 2**
- Calvin reads "let our prayer fall before thee" as a Hebrew idiom for a humble request. He thinks they mentioned their small numbers to win the prophet's pity, flattering him because they were double-minded. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-42.html
- Matthew Henry hears them saying they are unworthy to call God their own. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/42-3.html
- "Few of many" may echo Deuteronomy 28:62, where the people once promised to be as many as the stars were reduced for breaking the covenant. — https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-42
- **Was the request sincere? (a real disagreement)**
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes the request has been called hypocritical, but argues Jeremiah's prophecy treats it as earnest.
  - Keil and Delitzsch cite Nägelsbach, who called it hypocrisy and "a mere farce." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-2.htm
  - Coffman takes a middle view: they may truly have thought they wanted God's will while really wanting him to confirm their plan. We do not certainly know which it was. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-42.html

**v. 3**
- **"Your God" (another disagreement)**
  - Guzik quotes Kidner: the words "your God" are a small flaw that admitted more than the speakers realised. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
  - Calvin disagrees. They weren't distancing themselves from God; they were honouring Jeremiah as God's true prophet. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-42.html
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agrees with Calvin, and notes that Jeremiah replies "your God" (v. 4) and they answer "our God" (v. 6). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-2.htm
- Guzik quotes F. B. Meyer: believers often ask for prayer about a decision they have already made, hoping to bring God over to their side. He also quotes G. Campbell Morgan: prayer used to get our own way is superstition. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- Constable compares Zedekiah, who made a similar request and then disobeyed (37:3). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/42-3.html

**v. 4**
- Jeremiah had to seek God and pray. Guzik quotes Feinberg: he would not speak until he had the Lord's explicit word. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- Coffman notes Jeremiah had earlier been forbidden to pray for the people (7:16; 11:14; 14:11) but was now free to do so. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-42.html
- A homiletical commentary says disobeying after asking for and receiving clear light is worse than disobeying in ignorance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-42.html

**vv. 5–6**
- They swore a solemn oath to obey "whether it is pleasing or displeasing." They rightly expected blessing for obedience under the Old Covenant (Deuteronomy 28). Guzik cites John Trapp, who asked whether they were outright atheists to swear what they never meant to do. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- The Restoration Commentary says what follows proves they weren't sincere: they would follow God's word only so far as they agreed with it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-42.html

**v. 7**
- **Why ten days? (traditional and critical views differ)**
  - Guzik and the Clarke quotation he uses: prophecy came in God's timing; prophets could not prophesy whenever they liked. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
  - Benson: perhaps the delay punished their hypocrisy, or showed Jeremiah wasn't speaking on his own.
  - Barnes: it gave time to calm the panic after Gedaliah's murder.
  - Keil and Delitzsch: the delay was meant to discipline them, giving them time to reflect.
  - Hitzig and Graf (critical scholars): Jeremiah took ten days to mature his own conviction. Keil calls this unscriptural because it denies inspiration.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-7.htm
- Matthew Henry: to know the Lord's mind we must wait as well as pray. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- Keil and Delitzsch: Jeremiah gathered the captains and all the people and spoke in the name of the God to whom they had sent him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott hears an echo of Jeremiah's call in 1:10 ("to build and to plant"). Jeremiah's advice had always been to accept God's punishment rather than run to plans of their own. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm
- **"I relent / repent"** (on the same page):
  - Ellicott: not regret, but a change from judgment to mercy.
  - Barnes: divine justice had been satisfied.
  - Gill: not that God changed his mind, but that he changed his course of providence "according to his unchangeable will."
  - Pulpit: no change in God's nature or purpose, only in his conduct toward people, so the word is used by analogy (compare 1 Samuel 15:29).
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: staying meant living under Babylon, whose rule God had appointed, so to resist Babylon was to resist God.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm
- Guzik quotes Thompson: the Septuagint's "I relent" means the judgment already suffered had satisfied what the broken covenant required. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/

**v. 11**
- Keil and Delitzsch: repeating "do not fear him" adds special emphasis. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm
- Matthew Henry: whatever loss we fear from obeying, God's word has already provided against it. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: before Jerusalem fell the message was "surrender to exile"; now, in a season of mercy, it was "trust Me and stay." He quotes Thompson: there is no evidence Nebuchadnezzar avenged Gedaliah's murder. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/

**vv. 13–14**
- Calvin: God saw their hidden plans and answered them before they asked. Hoping for rest in Egypt while expecting trouble where God told them to stay was to charge God with lying. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-42.html
- A homiletical commentary links this to the standing ban on returning to Egypt (Deuteronomy 17:16). It notes that Egypt's own troubles were just beginning. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-42.html
- The Pulpit Commentary recalls that their ancestors went to Egypt for bread and ended in bondage. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-42.html

**v. 15**
- Gill: "set your faces" expresses their fixed, stubborn resolve. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-15.htm
- Matthew Henry: they thought that being a remnant meant they were bound to be spared. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_042.cfm

**vv. 16–17**
- What they feared in Judah would find them in Egypt. Guzik quotes Trapp: even fertile Egypt could know famine at God's word. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- Matthew Henry applies it generally: people who change places to escape life's troubles find the same troubles wherever they go. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_042.cfm

**v. 18**
- Calvin: the people had just seen Jeremiah proved right about Jerusalem, so they should believe this second threat too. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-42.html
- Constable: they would become a terrible object lesson and never return to the Promised Land. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-42.html
- **Scholarly note.** The Cambridge Bible treats vv. 15–18 as added by a later writer (a "supplementer"). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-19.htm

**v. 19**
- Keil and Delitzsch: God's own reply ends at v. 18; vv. 19–22 are Jeremiah's closing appeal. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-10.htm
- Benson: the word translated "admonished" can mean to warn before witnesses. He notes Moses had forbidden dealings with Egypt, and that fleeing there meant refusing the rule God had given Babylon (27:6). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-19.htm
- Gill: they could no longer plead ignorance. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-19.htm
- **Catholic translation.** The Douay-Rheims renders the end of the verse "I have adjured you this day." — https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/42-19.htm

**v. 20**
- **"Deceived yourselves" (translation and meaning differ)**
  - Geneva Bible notes: they were "hypocrites," set on Egypt whatever God said.
  - Gill and Poole: the deceit could be toward God, toward the prophet, or toward their own souls.
  - Barnes: an act of self-delusion; they were sure God would approve Egypt.
  - Pulpit: hypocrisy is "certainly not" the charge; rather, they had gone astray at the risk of their lives.
  - Keil and Delitzsch: "you err at the risk of your souls."
  - Cambridge prefers the Septuagint wording, "ye have done evil against" yourselves.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-20.htm

**v. 21**
- Keil and Delitzsch: the Hebrew past tense in vv. 20–21 presents their disobedience as already certain. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-20.htm
- Benson: Jeremiah knew they wouldn't obey because God had shown him their intentions. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-20.htm
- Constable: Jeremiah expected disobedience because of how they had responded before. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-42.html

**v. 22**
- Guzik: their insincere seeking only added to their guilt. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-42/
- Benson: they would die by the very deaths they went to Egypt to avoid. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/42-20.htm
- Ligonier ties this to 44:11–14: barely a remnant of that generation would return. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/trouble-egypt

**Catholic background (not tied to one verse)**
- Haydock's introduction to Jeremiah, quoting Challoner, mentions an ancient Hebrew tradition that the Jews who fled to Egypt stoned Jeremiah to death. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah.html
